questions: What are the signs of skin cancer?
What should I watch for?
When should I seek care?
My wound is not healing
My spot is bleeding
My skin lesion is growing
answer: A new growth, a sore that does not heal, or a spot that grows, bleeds, crusts or changes needs assessment by a trained health professional. This is especially important for people with albinism. Please seek care promptly; an app cannot diagnose the cause.

questions: How can I protect my skin from the sun?
How do I prevent sun damage?
Do I need sunscreen?
answer: Try to stay in the shade, especially around midday. Wear a wide-brimmed hat, protective clothing and sunglasses. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen SPF 30 or higher and reapply it as directed, especially outdoors. Sunscreen is one part of protection, not a reason to stay in strong sun longer.

questions: Why is skin cancer a risk for people with albinism?
What is albinism?
answer: Albinism reduces the amount of melanin that protects skin from sunlight. People with albinism can therefore develop sun damage and skin cancers, especially when sun protection or early treatment is difficult to access. Regular skin checks and sun protection are important.

questions: What does suspicious mean?
What does less suspicious mean?
Is SkinX a diagnosis?
answer: SkinX is an experimental screening tool, not a diagnosis. A 'Suspicious' result means you should seek clinical assessment. A 'Less suspicious' result does not rule out cancer. A changing, painful, bleeding or non-healing spot should still be checked by a professional. 'Cannot infer' currently means the image could not be processed.

questions: What is squamous cell carcinoma?
What is SCC?
answer: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a type of skin cancer that may look like a growing lump, scaly patch or sore that does not heal. It needs assessment by a health professional; appearance alone cannot confirm it.

questions: What is basal cell carcinoma?
What is BCC?
answer: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a type of skin cancer. It can appear as a new bump, a shiny or pink area, or a sore that repeatedly heals and returns. A clinician needs to examine any concerning spot.

questions: What is actinic keratosis?
Is AK cancer?
answer: Actinic keratosis (AK) is a sun-damaged patch that may feel rough or scaly. Some patches can progress to skin cancer, so a health professional should assess and treat them appropriately. SkinX cannot confirm AK from a photo.

questions: What is melanoma?
Can people with albinism get melanoma?
answer: Melanoma is a type of skin cancer. It can sometimes have little or no dark pigment. Any new, changing or concerning lesion should be examined. SkinX cannot identify melanoma as a separate diagnosis.

questions: How often should I check my skin?
Who should I visit?
answer: Regularly look for new or changing areas of skin. If possible, ask a trained health professional how often you need a full skin check. If a sore is not healing or a spot is changing, do not wait for a routine check.

questions: Why is my wound not healing?
I have a sore that will not heal
My skin has had a wound for weeks
answer: A sore or wound that does not heal needs assessment by a health professional. Persistent sores can have several causes, including skin cancer. Arrange a clinical check promptly even if an app says Less suspicious.

questions: A spot on my skin is bleeding
Why does my skin spot bleed?
My lesion bleeds when I touch it
answer: A skin spot that bleeds repeatedly, grows or becomes an open sore should be checked by a health professional promptly. Do not rely on an image screening result to decide whether to seek care.

questions: My skin bump is growing
Is a growing skin spot dangerous?
A mole is changing size
answer: A new or growing skin spot should be examined by a health professional. Changes can have different causes, and a photo or chatbot cannot tell you what it is.

questions: What should I do after sunburn?
My skin is red after the sun
How can I avoid sunburn?
answer: Move out of the sun and protect the affected skin. Keep the skin cool and hydrated. Seek medical care for severe burns, widespread blistering, fever, or feeling unwell. Prevent further exposure using clothing, shade and sunscreen.

questions: How often do I apply sunscreen?
How much sunscreen should I use?
Should I reapply sunscreen?
answer: Use a generous amount of broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin. Reapply about every two hours when outdoors and after swimming or sweating. Hats, clothing and shade remain important.

questions: What clothes protect me from the sun?
Is a hat enough?
How can I protect myself without sunscreen?
answer: Wear tightly woven long sleeves, trousers, a wide-brimmed hat and sunglasses. Seek shade, especially when sunlight is strong. Clothing and sunscreen can be used together.

questions: What does SPF 30 mean?
Which sunscreen should I choose?
Is sunscreen necessary for albinism?
answer: Choose broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, where available. Sunscreen reduces ultraviolet exposure but does not block all radiation, so use shade and protective clothing too.

questions: What is a precancerous lesion?
Can a rough patch turn into cancer?
What does precancer mean?
answer: Some sun-damaged skin changes, such as actinic keratosis, can develop into cancer. They should be assessed by a health professional. SkinX cannot confirm whether a patch is precancerous.

questions: How do I examine my skin?
How can I check for skin cancer?
What should I watch for on my skin?
answer: Look for new, changing, bleeding or non-healing spots. Ask someone you trust to help check areas that are difficult to see, if you are comfortable. A health worker can advise on a professional skin examination.

questions: Where can I get a skin lesion checked?
Should I visit a clinic or dermatologist?
What happens at a skin consultation?
answer: A clinician at a health centre or hospital can examine a concerning skin change and refer you to a dermatologist when needed. Explain how long the spot has been there and whether it has grown, bled or failed to heal.

questions: What is a skin biopsy?
How is skin cancer diagnosed?
Can a picture confirm skin cancer?
answer: A clinician may need to examine a skin spot and take a small tissue sample called a biopsy. Laboratory assessment can help confirm the diagnosis. SkinX photographs cannot replace a biopsy or clinical examination.

questions: Can I use SkinX without internet?
Is screening offline?
Does SkinX need mobile data?
answer: SkinX screening and saved educational answers run on this phone without internet. Cloud accounts and optional online AI require a working connection.

questions: Does SkinX upload my pictures?
Are my screening photos stored online?
Is my information private?
answer: The offline screening model runs on your phone. SkinX does not need to upload a photo for local screening. Check any future cloud-sharing option and privacy notice before choosing to share health information.

questions: Should I take another photo?
Why does SkinX say cannot infer?
What if a photo is rejected?
answer: Cannot infer means the app could not use that photo or complete its screening. Try a clear photo of the affected skin in good light. A changing or non-healing lesion still needs a clinician even when screening fails.

questions: How should I photograph my skin?
How to take a good lesion photo?
Can I take a photo in bad light?
answer: Use bright, even light and hold the phone steady. Keep the skin change visible and in focus. Avoid filters and include enough surrounding skin to see the area. A good photo still cannot confirm a diagnosis.

questions: My skin spot itches or hurts
Does skin cancer always hurt?
What if my mole is painful?
answer: Some skin changes cause pain or itching and others do not. Symptoms alone cannot confirm or rule out cancer. Have a new, changing or persistent spot examined by a health professional.

questions: Can skin cancer be pink?
Does a lesion need to be dark?
Can melanoma have no color?
answer: Some skin cancers can look pink, pale or skin-colored rather than dark. This includes some melanomas. A new or changing spot should be checked regardless of its color.

questions: Can SkinX tell me which cancer I have?
Can SkinX tell SCC from BCC?
Is a less suspicious result safe?
answer: SkinX is a research screening tool that flags patterns as Suspicious or Less suspicious; it does not identify a definite disease or confirm that a lesion is safe. Ask a clinician about any concern.

questions: How can I help someone with albinism protect their skin?
How do I support my child with albinism?
answer: Help provide shade, protective clothes, hats and sunscreen when available. Encourage timely skin checks without blame or stigma. A health professional can offer advice appropriate to the person’s age and situation.

questions: Do people with albinism need sunglasses?
How can I protect my eyes from sunlight?
answer: Sunglasses that block ultraviolet light and wide-brimmed hats can help protect the eyes from the sun. An eye-care professional can advise on vision needs linked to albinism.

questions: What if I cannot afford a dermatologist?
Where should I go if a specialist is far away?
answer: Start with a nearby health centre or qualified health worker and explain your skin concern. They can assess the spot and advise whether referral is needed. Do not delay care for a sore that bleeds, grows or does not heal.
